desc:
I found an article that said "The microwave was invented to heat hamsters humanely in 1950s experiments." And I thought, no it wasn't. ...was it?

Pull down the description for thorough references and credits.

Thanks to James Lovelock for his time! His latest book is Novacene: https://amzn.to/3hmKsWz [that is, of course, an Amazon affiliate link]
 
Filmed safely: https://www.tomscott.com/safe/ -

recs.stt: Frozen in Siberian Permafrost for 24,000 Years, Microscopic Animal Comes to Life
recs.x:
They already studied this. It sometimes worked with small animals like mice, but fails as organisms get larger. There was a really interesting video about how microwaves were first used to test this:
 [link]

recs.x:
That's purely a size thing iirc. Lot quicker to get enough heat into a mouse to thaw it, than a human.

Edit to add an interesting related video: [link]
This Tom Scott's video from last year about microwave ovens features a nice interview with Lovelock: [link]

Despite everything else he accomplished in his quite storied professional career as one of the last independent scientists... Including his work on the Viking mars landers! [link] 

To me he will always be the man who invented his own microwave to thaw frozen hamsters. The whole story is worth a watch since Tom Scott does an admirable job of explaining how he went digging up a weird fact expecting to debunk it only to wind up recording an amazing interview with James Lovelock [link] but if you’re impatient the interview with lovelock about cryopreserved hamsters and his "microwave" starts here

Tom Scott interviewed him last year in a really wonderful video about microwaves.

recs.x:
Tom Scott made a great video about it, he even got to the guy who started using microwaves for thawing entire small animals. Before microwaves (diathermic heating) they would use a hot piece of metal, like a large spoon.

 [link]

recs.stt: FastVideo: a lightweight framework for accelerating large video diffusion models
recs.x:
actually really easy to do that with hamsters, but it turns out scaling the process up isn't so easy (Tom Scott has a good video tangentially related to this[2]). I think a lot of people are standing near the top of the steep part of a sigmoid curve and saying "Wow look how far we've come in just 3 years! The next 3 years are going to be insane!" When in reality we just have a long plateau of minor improvements in front of us. But who knows, maybe that next breakthrough is right around the corner.
